title: Information Geometry Loss for Time Series Forecasting
one_liner: Teach the model to predict distributions correctly by measuring distance between prediction shapes, not just comparing single numbers.
lead: When you forecast the future (like predicting tomorrow's temperature), you need to guess not just one number but a range of possibilities. Most forecasting models use loss functions (ways to measure if the guess was wrong) that compare predictions to real values point-by-point, like comparing a single number to another single number. This ignores the shape of the full prediction—the spread, the asymmetry, the tails. This paper introduces a smarter loss that measures how different two complete predictions are by treating them as shapes in a specially-warped space where the axes adjust based on how sensitive each part of the shape is to small changes.

problem.h2: Comparing prediction shapes as if they were single numbers
paras: When forecasting the future, the model outputs not a single guess but a full distribution (a shape showing how likely each possible value is). A good forecast distribution has the right center, the right spread, and the right shape overall. But standard loss functions measure distance between predictions and reality by treating them as single points: they compute the average squared error between the predicted mean and the true value. This is like measuring how far two mountain peaks are apart by only looking at their height difference, ignoring whether the mountains have steep or gentle slopes.

A naive forecaster might learn to predict a narrow, confident distribution even when the future is uncertain, because point-wise metrics reward being close to the average and do not penalize overconfidence. The model learns the wrong shape. For tasks that require accurate uncertainty (like medical forecasts or safety-critical predictions), this is dangerous.

callout.b: The paper's method in one sentence.
callout.html: Measure the distance between predicted and true distributions as geometric shapes in a high-dimensional space, rather than comparing single numbers.

steps.b: Output numbers that describe the shape
steps.text: The model outputs learnable numbers that fully describe a probability distribution: the center (mean), the spread (variance), and how lopsided it is (skew parameters).
This metric measures how sensitive the distribution is to tiny changes in those parameters; it captures the geometric 'stretching' of the probability space.
Instead of comparing single values, compare how far the predicted distribution sits from the true distribution in this geometric space.
Use Bregman divergence to capture asymmetric errors (e.g., overestimating is worse than underestimating, or vice versa).
Compute how to nudge the model's weights by considering the curvature of the space (how the loss surface bends), not just the direction of steepest descent.

paras: The paper changes the loss function: the method the model uses to measure how wrong its forecast was. Instead of comparing single numbers (predicted mean vs. true value), it compares entire probability distributions by measuring their geometric distance on a statistical manifold (a high-dimensional surface where each point represents a different distribution shape).

hidden.name: Geometric distance between distributions
paras: The hidden quantity is the true distance between the predicted distribution and the true distribution, measured not by straightforward subtraction but in a specially-warped space where the measurement scales depend on how sensitive the distribution is to each parameter. This distance captures not just the difference in means, but also differences in spread, skewness, and tail behavior.

The paper estimates this distance by computing the Fisher information matrix—a table of numbers that shows how much the distribution shape changes when you adjust each parameter—and using it to reweight the comparison. This warped distance penalizes not just getting the center wrong, but getting the shape wrong: a narrow, overconfident prediction is heavily penalized if the truth is spread out, because changing from narrow to spread is a big move in the warped space.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger effect on model learning. Highlighted cells show what Fisher information captures that old MSE misses.

reads.html: The model learns by measuring how different its full prediction shape is from reality, not just whether the center point is close.
The Fisher information metric on the statistical manifold defines an intrinsic distance between predicted and true distributions, enabling asymmetric penalization of errors in shape and calibration.

paras: Standard loss functions measure straight-line distance between the predicted mean and the true value in one-dimensional space. This ignores the fact that a probability distribution is a multi-dimensional object: it has a center, a width, a skew (lopsidedness), and tails (extreme values). When you use straight-line distance, a model can minimize the loss by predicting a narrow distribution close to the average, even when the truth requires a wide, spread-out distribution. Standard loss measures only whether the center is correct and ignores spread entirely, so the model learns overconfidence because the loss signal never penalizes being too confident: it only checks if the center is right.

The Fisher information matrix re-measures distance in a space where the axes are naturally scaled by how sensitive the distribution is to changes in each parameter. A small change in the variance parameter (how spread out the distribution is) is treated as a large distance in this warped space, because changing the spread dramatically changes the entire distribution shape. A small change in the mean is treated proportionally, based on how much it affects the distribution. Now, when a model tries to get the spread wrong, the loss function pushes back much harder. The model learns that predicting the wrong shape is expensive because the distance in the warped space makes it obvious.

Additionally, the paper adds a Bregman divergence component, which can assign different penalties to errors in different directions. For example, if underestimating is worse than overestimating in your domain (like weather forecasts where underpredicting rain is more costly), the loss can be tuned to reflect that asymmetry.

stages.s: True future value and predicted distribution parameters
Parameterize predicted distribution with learnable statistics
Measure distributional distance in warped space
Loss value; compute which way to nudge weights using curvature-aware descent

math.words: Total loss equals the distributional distance in the warped information-geometry space, measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence weighted by Fisher information, plus an asymmetric penalty term using Bregman divergence.
math.equation: L = D_F(p_pred || p_true) + lambda * D_Breg(p_true, p_pred)
symbols: Fisher information distance between predicted and true distributions
the true distribution (from the observed data)
weighting parameter that controls how much to penalize asymmetric errors

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the true distribution is centered at 10 with variance 4 (fairly spread out).
The model predicts mean 10, variance 1 (narrow and confident, but wrong spread).
Standard MSE loss: (10-10)^2 = 0. The model is 'perfect' even though the shape is wrong.
Fisher distance: Fisher(1) = 1 / (variance^2) = 1 / 1 = 1. Fisher(4) = 1/16 = 0.0625. The difference in scaling is large, so the distance is penalized heavily.
InfoGeo loss: approximately 0.4 (simplified; captures the huge shape mismatch).
Result: gradient points the model toward predicting variance 4, not staying at variance 1.

math.note: The Fisher matrix re-scales the space so that changes to spread are treated as large moves (because changing the spread dramatically changes the entire distribution shape) and changes to mean are treated proportionally. Since the model's loss increases sharply when spread is wrong in this warped space, the gradient points strongly toward predicting the correct spread instead of ignoring it.

charts.title: Old method (straight-line distance loss)
charts.note: Straight-line distance loss gets the center right but the spread completely wrong. The model learns overconfidence.

charts.title: This paper (InfoGeo)
charts.note: InfoGeo learns both center and shape correctly, producing honest uncertainty bands that actually match reality.

items.html: If the model predicts a distribution with near-zero variance, the Fisher matrix becomes very large and can cause training instability. The paper addresses this by gently steering (adding a small penalty to keep variance from going too small), but aggressive training steps can still cause the numbers to blow up.

items.b: Fisher metric assumes smooth, well-behaved distributions.
items.html: If the true data distribution is multimodal (has multiple peaks) or heavy-tailed, the single-peak distribution parameterization may not be flexible enough, and the Fisher metric may not correctly capture the true distance.

items.b: Computational cost of computing Fisher information.
items.html: Computing and storing the Fisher matrix scales with the dimension of the distribution parameters. For very high-dimensional problems or long sequences, this can be expensive compared to standard MSE.

items.b: Done right: carefully scale the learning rate, ensure the distribution family can express the true data, and use low-rank approximations of the Fisher matrix for large-scale problems.
items.html: The paper shows that with these precautions, the method is stable across seven datasets and five architectures.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time series forecaster (e.g., on synthetic data or a standard benchmark like electricity load forecasting). Train one version with standard MSE loss and another with InfoGeo loss. At test time, for each time step, compute the predicted distribution (mean and variance) and the calibration: does the true future value fall inside the predicted confidence band (say, mean plus-or-minus one standard deviation) roughly 68% of the time? Measure how often the true value falls in the 95% confidence band (mean plus-or-minus two standard deviations) — it should be roughly 95%. Also measure the average predicted variance: is it realistic, or is one model overconfident?
demo.metric_eq: Calibration error = | (fraction of samples in 68% band) - 0.68 | + | (fraction of samples in 95% band) - 0.95 |
demo.closing: The demo should make impossible to miss: InfoGeo's predicted uncertainty bands actually match the frequency of true surprises, while MSE's bands are too narrow because the model learned overconfidence.
